text: By ending your membership you will lose access to your Prime benefits.
rationale: Explicit loss framing in the cancellation flow. Emphasizes what user will lose rather than neutral confirmation. Designed to trigger loss aversion and discourage cancellation.
risk_outcome: User abandons cancellation due to fear of losing benefits

text: Paige, do you still want to end your Prime for Young Adults benefits?
rationale: Personalized guilt-tripping using first name. Reframes cancellation as 'ending benefits' rather than 'stopping charges'. Creates emotional friction.
risk_outcome: User feels personally addressed and guilty about canceling

text: You still have 13 days left to enjoy your Prime for Young Adults benefits until the next billing cycle
rationale: Reminds user of remaining paid time to create sunk cost feeling. Implies waste if they cancel now. Borderline - could be seen as helpful info.
risk_outcome: User delays cancellation and forgets, gets charged again

text: By cancelling, you will lose access to 5% back on eligible purchases with your Prime Visa. You've earned $87.70 from 5% back over the last 12 statements, and you will keep your already-earned rewards.
rationale: Classic sunk cost manipulation. Shows specific dollar amount ($87.70) user has 'earned' to make cancellation feel like throwing away money. The earned value anchor makes continuing feel like protecting an investment.
risk_outcome: User keeps subscription to avoid 'losing' the cashback benefit

text: By cancelling, you will no longer be eligible for your unclaimed Prime exclusive offers.
rationale: Vague threat about losing 'unclaimed offers' without specifying what they are. Creates FOMO about unknown future value. User can't evaluate what they're actually losing.
risk_outcome: User worries about missing unknown valuable offers

text: If you cancel, you will immediately lose your remaining words: 16,768
rationale: Explicit threat of immediate loss of paid credits. Uses specific number (16,768) to make loss feel concrete and painful. Red warning icon and text color amplify urgency. Classic sunk cost manipulation.
risk_outcome: User abandons cancellation to avoid losing credits they already paid for

text: Are you sure you want to cancel? We have new updates every week that keep you at the forefront of AI tech.
rationale: Creates FOMO about vague future features. No specific dates or concrete features promised. Implies user will fall behind competitors if they cancel. Roadmap shown without timelines.
risk_outcome: User stays subscribed waiting for features that may never arrive

text: Opt for a subscription pause instead of canceling, and unlock a bonus of 10,000 free word credits the moment you return!
rationale: Incentivizes pause over cancel. Pause keeps user in billing system and easier to resume charges. The 'bonus' creates obligation to return. Framed as benefit but maintains subscription relationship.
risk_outcome: User pauses instead of cancels, forgets, and gets charged when pause ends

text: Get FREE Two-Day Shipping
rationale: FTC cited this as Interface Interference. Prominent button emphasized 'FREE' shipping while hiding that clicking enrolls user in $14.99/month auto-renewing Prime subscription. Option to decline was comparatively inconspicuous link.
risk_outcome: User unknowingly enrolls in $139/year subscription thinking they are just getting free shipping on one order
case_citation: FTC v. Amazon.com Inc., Case No. 2:23-cv-0932-JHC (W.D. Wash. 2023)

text: No thanks, I don't want FREE Two-Day Shipping
rationale: FTC cited as Confirmshaming. Decline option used emotive language to guilt users. Framing declining Prime as rejecting 'FREE' shipping rather than declining paid subscription. Settlement specifically banned this language.
risk_outcome: User feels foolish declining 'free' benefit, enrolls in subscription they don't want
case_citation: FTC v. Amazon.com Inc., Case No. 2:23-cv-0932-JHC (W.D. Wash. 2023)

text: Start your 30-day free trial
rationale: FTC alleged Amazon engaged in Sneaking by hiding or delaying disclosure of Prime's price and auto-renewal feature. Material terms like $14.99/month charge after trial buried in small font while 'free trial' emphasized.
risk_outcome: User enrolls in trial without understanding auto-renewal at $14.99/month
case_citation: FTC v. Amazon.com Inc., Case No. 2:23-cv-0932-JHC (W.D. Wash. 2023)

text: Are you sure? You'll lose FREE Two-Day Shipping on millions of items
rationale: Part of Amazon's 'Iliad Flow' cancellation process. FTC cited this as Obstruction/Roach Motel technique. Multiple pages of loss-framing designed to thwart cancellation. Required 4-page, 6-click, 15-option flow to cancel.
risk_outcome: User abandons cancellation due to fear of losing benefits
case_citation: FTC v. Amazon.com Inc., Case No. 2:23-cv-0932-JHC (W.D. Wash. 2023)

text: Keep my benefits
rationale: Prominent button in cancellation flow. FTC cited asymmetric presentation - 'Keep benefits' button prominent while cancel option less visible. Part of Iliad Flow obstruction pattern.
risk_outcome: User clicks prominent button to stop annoying flow, accidentally keeps subscription
case_citation: FTC v. Amazon.com Inc., Case No. 2:23-cv-0932-JHC (W.D. Wash. 2023)

text: Remind me later
rationale: Diversionary option in cancellation flow. FTC cited multiple diversions including discount offers, benefit reminders, and delay options designed to prevent completion of cancellation.
risk_outcome: User postpones cancellation, forgets, gets charged again
case_citation: FTC v. Amazon.com Inc., Case No. 2:23-cv-0932-JHC (W.D. Wash. 2023)

text: You'll lose access to Prime Video, including thousands of movies and TV shows
rationale: Loss framing in cancellation flow. Part of 15-option obstruction flow. Emphasizes loss of streaming content to discourage cancellation.
risk_outcome: User abandons cancellation to keep video access
case_citation: FTC v. Amazon.com Inc., Case No. 2:23-cv-0932-JHC (W.D. Wash. 2023)

text: Easy Cancellation – If your family does not love ABCmouse, you can cancel at any time!
rationale: FTC found this claim deceptive. Despite promising 'Easy Cancellation', actual cancellation required navigating confusing multi-page process with promotions designed to prevent completion. Hundreds of thousands of consumers who visited cancellation path remained subscribed.
risk_outcome: User signs up believing cancellation is easy when it is actually designed to be difficult
case_citation: FTC v. Age of Learning Inc., No. 2:20-cv-7996 (C.D. Cal. 2020)

text: Special Offer: 12 months for $59.95
rationale: FTC alleged this failed to disclose that subscription would automatically renew indefinitely at full price. No clear disclosure that $59.95 charge would repeat annually without action. Relied on hyperlinked terms and conditions for disclosure.
risk_outcome: User charged $59.95 annually without realizing subscription auto-renews
case_citation: FTC v. Age of Learning Inc., No. 2:20-cv-7996 (C.D. Cal. 2020)

text: Continue your learning journey - Extend your membership now!
rationale: FTC cited cluttered cancellation pages with advertisements and promotions aimed at convincing consumer not to cancel. If consumer clicked any promotional link, cancellation process stopped and they had to start over.
risk_outcome: User accidentally clicks promotion, loses progress in cancellation flow
case_citation: FTC v. Age of Learning Inc., No. 2:20-cv-7996 (C.D. Cal. 2020)

text: Your child has earned 847 tickets and unlocked 23 prizes! Keep their progress going.
rationale: Sunk cost manipulation targeting parents through children's achievements. FTC noted cancellation path included multiple pages of promotional content designed to prevent cancellation completion.
risk_outcome: Parent abandons cancellation to preserve child's virtual rewards
case_citation: FTC v. Age of Learning Inc., No. 2:20-cv-7996 (C.D. Cal. 2020)

text: To cancel your service, please call our retention team at [phone number]
rationale: FTC found Vonage allowed easy online signup but forced phone-only cancellation starting 2017. Phone number was obscured on website, hours limited, and calls frequently dropped. Internal email said customers were 'sent in a circle when they want to downgrade or remove the service.'
risk_outcome: User cannot cancel online despite signing up online, must navigate phone maze
case_citation: FTC v. Vonage Holdings Corp., No. 3:22-cv-06435 (D.N.J. 2022)

text: Before you go, let me tell you about some great offers that could save you money
rationale: FTC cited lengthy sales pitches during cancellation calls. Retention agents were given monetary incentives to prevent cancellations. Customers endured repeated pitches before being allowed to cancel.
risk_outcome: User gives up on cancellation due to exhausting phone process
case_citation: FTC v. Vonage Holdings Corp., No. 3:22-cv-06435 (D.N.J. 2022)

text: Your early termination fee will be $[amount]
rationale: FTC found early termination fees were not clearly disclosed at signup but surprised customers during cancellation. Sometimes totaled hundreds of dollars. Constituted 'junk fees' designed to deter cancellation.
risk_outcome: User keeps unwanted service to avoid unexpected fee
case_citation: FTC v. Vonage Holdings Corp., No. 3:22-cv-06435 (D.N.J. 2022)

text: Your cancellation request has been processed
rationale: FTC found Vonage continued charging customers AFTER they received cancellation confirmation. When customers complained, they received only partial refunds. This constituted unauthorized billing.
risk_outcome: User believes service is cancelled but continues to be charged
case_citation: FTC v. Vonage Holdings Corp., No. 3:22-cv-06435 (D.N.J. 2022)

text: Order Now to Enter!
rationale: FTC found Publishers Clearing House used dark patterns to mislead consumers about how to enter sweepstakes. Made consumers believe purchase was necessary to enter when free entry was available but obscured.
risk_outcome: User makes unnecessary purchase believing it is required for sweepstakes entry
case_citation: FTC v. Publishers Clearing House LLC (2023)

text: Your entry has been processed. Complete your order to finalize.
rationale: FTC alleged PCH made it appear purchase completion was necessary for sweepstakes entry. $18.5M settlement for deceptive negative option marketing.
risk_outcome: User completes purchase thinking it finalizes sweepstakes entry
case_citation: FTC v. Publishers Clearing House LLC (2023)

text: Limited Time Offer - Enroll Now Before Rates Increase!
rationale: FTC cited false urgency in health insurance marketing. $100M settlement for deceptive practices including fake limited-time offers. Rates were not actually increasing.
risk_outcome: User enrolls hastily in unsuitable insurance plan due to fake deadline
case_citation: FTC v. Benefytt Technologies Inc. (2022)

text: Only 3 spots remaining at this price!
rationale: FTC found Benefytt used fabricated scarcity claims to pressure enrollment. Part of $100M settlement for deceptive enrollment practices.
risk_outcome: User enrolls without proper comparison shopping due to fake scarcity
case_citation: FTC v. Benefytt Technologies Inc. (2022)

text: You're Pre-Approved!
rationale: FTC found Credit Karma deceived consumers with false pre-approval claims. Users were told they were pre-approved but then rejected after providing personal information. $3M settlement.
risk_outcome: User shares personal/financial data expecting approval that doesn't exist
case_citation: FTC v. Credit Karma LLC (2022)

text: 90% approval odds - Apply now!
rationale: FTC internal A/B testing showed 'Excellent odds' language increased clicks. Company chose deceptive claim despite knowing users were rejected at much higher rates.
risk_outcome: User applies expecting approval, damages credit score with rejection
case_citation: FTC v. Credit Karma LLC (2022)

text: No thanks, I don't want to save money
rationale: Classic confirmshaming pattern documented on deceptive.design. Decline option forces user to self-identify as someone who dislikes saving money. Creates social identity threat to deter opting out of marketing emails.
risk_outcome: User signs up for unwanted marketing emails to avoid self-shaming

text: No, I prefer to pay full price
rationale: Confirmshaming pattern from deceptive.design Hall of Shame. Opt-out is framed as an irrational financial choice. Forces user to affirm they prefer paying more, creating cognitive dissonance that drives sign-up.
risk_outcome: User provides email to avoid feeling foolish about declining discount

text: No, I don't want to stay alive
rationale: Extreme confirmshaming from MyMedic.com (2018) documented in deceptive.design Hall of Shame. Opt-out label equates declining a newsletter with choosing death. Exploits mortality fear for email capture. Particularly harmful given target audience of first responders.
risk_outcome: User surrenders email under extreme emotional duress from death-framing

text: I don't read.
rationale: Confirmshaming from Esquire documented on deceptive.design. Declining the newsletter is framed as illiteracy. Weaponizes intellectual identity to guilt users into subscribing.
risk_outcome: User subscribes to avoid being labeled as someone who does not read

text: No, I REALLY hate saving money
rationale: Intensified confirmshaming documented on deceptive.design. Capitalized emphasis on 'REALLY' doubles down on shaming. User must not only decline but emphatically affirm an irrational preference.
risk_outcome: User submits email to avoid affirming exaggerated irrational identity

text: Hurry up! Sale ending in 11 Hrs, 59 Mins, 46 Sec. Sale Ends Once The Timer Hits Zero!
rationale: Fake countdown timer from Shopify 'Hurrify' app documented on deceptive.design. Timer is configured to loop infinitely when it reaches zero (evergreen mode). The urgency is entirely fabricated.
risk_outcome: User makes impulse purchase under false time pressure that does not actually exist

text: Limited time only
rationale: Fake limited-time message from Samsung documented on deceptive.design. The offer ran continuously for months (Nov-Dec 2022) and actually increased in value. No real deadline existed despite 'limited time' framing.
risk_outcome: User rushes purchase believing deal will expire when it is perpetually available

text: Only 2 rooms left at this price!
rationale: Fake scarcity message commonly seen on booking platforms, documented on deceptive.design. Stock numbers are often fabricated or algorithmically generated on each page load, not reflecting real inventory.
risk_outcome: User books immediately without comparison shopping due to fabricated scarcity

text: 3 other people are looking at this right now
rationale: Fake social proof / activity message documented on deceptive.design. Creates artificial competitive pressure by claiming others are viewing the same item. Numbers are often randomly generated or grossly inflated.
risk_outcome: User rushes to purchase fearing someone else will buy the item first

text: Sale ends soon
rationale: Vague urgency message from Chicwish documented in Princeton/Chicago deceptive patterns study cited on deceptive.design. No end date specified, withholding information to create open-ended anxiety. Sale remains active indefinitely.
risk_outcome: User purchases hastily under vague deadline that never materializes

text: Only 1 left in stock — order soon
rationale: Fake low-stock warning documented on deceptive.design. Amazon and similar platforms show persistent low-stock labels that do not reflect actual inventory. Princeton study found some sites randomly generated stock numbers on each page load.
risk_outcome: User makes impulse purchase to avoid missing out on falsely scarce item

text: Lightning Deal — Limited Time Offer!
rationale: Amazon Lightning Deal urgency pattern documented on deceptive.design. Countdown timers and scarcity labels create artificial pressure. Actual availability often far exceeds what is implied by the urgency framing.
risk_outcome: User skips comparison shopping and purchases impulsively under fabricated deadline

text: To cancel your subscription, please contact our support team
rationale: Hard-to-cancel pattern from the New York Times documented on deceptive.design. Despite easy online subscription, cancellation requires contacting support. Chat agents use scripted retention pitches. Creates asymmetric friction — the roach motel pattern.
risk_outcome: User gives up on cancellation due to friction and continues paying

text: To cancel, please call our retention team
rationale: Phone-only cancellation from Savage X Fenty documented on deceptive.design. The $49.95/month membership can only be cancelled by calling customer support, while sign-up is fully online. Classic roach motel asymmetry.
risk_outcome: User continues paying subscription because phone cancellation is too burdensome

text: Are you sure you want to leave? Your friends will miss you!
rationale: Emotional guilt trip in cancellation flows documented on deceptive.design. Combines hard-to-cancel obstruction with confirmshaming. Frames leaving as social abandonment to trigger loss aversion around relationships.
risk_outcome: User abandons account deletion to avoid perceived social loss

text: Service Fee: $24.50
rationale: Hidden costs pattern from Ticketmaster documented on deceptive.design. Base ticket price shown prominently; service fees, processing fees, and delivery fees only revealed at final checkout. By that point user has invested time selecting seats and entering details.
risk_outcome: User pays significantly more than advertised price due to drip pricing

text: Processing Fee: $8.95 | Facility Charge: $3.50 | Order Processing Fee: $5.00
rationale: Multiple hidden fees stacked at checkout, documented on deceptive.design. Each fee is individually small but collectively substantial. Splitting into many fees also makes comparison shopping impossible — a form of Comparison Prevention.
risk_outcome: User pays 30-40% more than expected due to stacked hidden fees

text: Sports Direct Mug + Magazine — £1.00
rationale: Sneak into basket from Sports Direct documented on deceptive.design and BBC Watchdog. Unwanted mug and magazine automatically added to cart without user consent. User must actively spot and remove the item, which is easily overlooked.
risk_outcome: User unknowingly pays for unrequested item bundled into cart

text: Added for your protection: 1 Year Security Software
rationale: Sneak into basket from Laptop Outlet documented on deceptive.design. Security software and mouse auto-added when purchasing laptop. 'Added for your protection' frames unwanted addition as a safety measure, exploiting authority claim.
risk_outcome: User pays for unwanted software and accessories auto-added to cart

text: Start your free trial — credit card required
rationale: Forced continuity pattern documented on deceptive.design. Credit card is collected for a 'free' trial with auto-renewal buried in terms. Exploits Status Quo bias — users who forget to cancel are automatically charged, as documented on Netflix and Hulu.
risk_outcome: User is auto-charged after forgetting to cancel before trial ends

text: $0 today, then $14.99/month
rationale: Forced continuity documented on deceptive.design. '$0 today' dominates visual hierarchy while recurring charge is de-emphasized. Anchors user on zero cost while obscuring ongoing financial commitment.
risk_outcome: User signs up perceiving zero cost, gets locked into monthly charges

text: Create an account to continue reading
rationale: Forced action pattern documented on deceptive.design. User wants to read content but is forced to create an account first, surrendering personal data. The account creation often includes hidden marketing consent and data sharing agreements.
risk_outcome: User shares personal data unnecessarily to access content

text: Use our app for the best experience
rationale: Nagging pattern from Reddit documented on deceptive.design. Persistent prompts push users to download the app despite clear disinterest. Implies inferior experience if they continue on web, creating mild fear of missing out.
risk_outcome: User downloads app granting broader device permissions than web browsing requires

text: We've alerted you multiple times that this printer had non-Original HP cartridges installed. This is your final notice to fix the issue.
rationale: Aggressive nagging from HP documented on deceptive.design Hall of Shame. Frames third-party cartridge use as a 'problem' user must 'fix'. Escalating threat language (multiple alerts, final notice) pressures purchase of expensive OEM cartridges.
risk_outcome: User buys overpriced OEM cartridges due to intimidating printer DRM messaging

text: Use this activity
rationale: Privacy zuckering from Facebook documented on deceptive.design. 'Use this activity' obscures that user is consenting to data collection and targeted advertising. Deliberately vague label avoids stating what the user is actually agreeing to.
risk_outcome: User consents to broad data collection without understanding the scope

text: Make Microsoft Edge your default browser for the best experience on Windows
rationale: Nagging pattern from Microsoft documented on deceptive.design Hall of Shame. Pop-ups appear during full-screen activities (e.g., gaming) to push Edge. Implies degraded experience unless user complies. Uses OS-level authority to pressure browser choice.
risk_outcome: User switches browser defaults due to persistent interruption, not informed choice

text: Annual plan, paid monthly
rationale: Hidden subscription commitment from Adobe documented on deceptive.design and DOJ lawsuit. 'Annual plan, paid monthly' obscures that user is locked into 12-month commitment. Early termination fee buried in fine print and optional text boxes.
risk_outcome: User believes they have a monthly plan but faces early termination fees

text: Sarah from New York just bought this item 2 minutes ago
rationale: Fake social proof activity notification documented on deceptive.design. Fabricated purchase notifications with fake names and locations create illusion of high demand. 87% of consumers report seeing these messages, per OECD survey.
risk_outcome: User purchases impulsively believing product is in high demand when activity is fabricated

text: Upgrade to Premium for the best experience
rationale: Comparison prevention documented on deceptive.design. Vague 'best experience' language avoids specifying what Premium includes that free/basic does not. Makes rational comparison impossible, pushing emotional decision-making.
risk_outcome: User upgrades to more expensive tier without understanding the actual differences

text: Share — Can edit
rationale: Sneaking pattern from Figma documented on deceptive.design Hall of Shame. Share button with 'Can edit' silently adds billable seats. Unlike Google Docs, sharing triggers per-seat charges. Corporate credit card holders often do not notice the incremental costs.
risk_outcome: Organization incurs unexpected seat charges from routine sharing actions

text: I would like to receive updates through the newsletter
rationale: Pre-selection dark pattern documented on deceptive.design. Checkbox is pre-selected by default so user is automatically opted into marketing emails. Users who do not notice or do not uncheck consent without informed decision.
risk_outcome: User unknowingly opts into marketing communications via pre-checked consent

text: Uncheck this box if you prefer not to not receive promotional emails
rationale: Trick question pattern documented on deceptive.design. Double negative ('prefer not to not receive') confuses user intent. Processing the sentence requires cognitive effort that most users will not invest during fast form completion.
risk_outcome: User makes unintended consent choice due to deliberately confusing language

text: Accept cookies to continue viewing this content
rationale: Cookie wall from HRAcuity documented on deceptive.design. Forces cookie acceptance to view a YouTube embed that does not require cookies. Forced action pattern — user must consent to tracking to access otherwise freely available content.
risk_outcome: User consents to unnecessary tracking to access content available without cookies

text: Your subscription has been automatically upgraded to the $99.99/year plan
rationale: Bait and switch from Microsoft documented on deceptive.design Hall of Shame. Users were silently upgraded to a more expensive subscription tier. Downgrading back required going through the full cancellation flow to find the original pricing option.
risk_outcome: User pays 43% more annually without consenting to the upgrade

text: Download
rationale: Disguised ad pattern documented on deceptive.design. Fake 'Download' button styled to look like the actual download CTA on software download sites. Clicking leads to ad/malware instead of intended file. Exploits UI familiarity and urgency.
risk_outcome: User installs unwanted software or malware believing they clicked legitimate download

text: Find friends already on the platform — import your contacts
rationale: Friend spam pattern from LinkedIn documented on deceptive.design. Contact import is framed as finding friends but actually sends mass invitations to entire address book. LinkedIn paid $13M in settlement over this practice.
risk_outcome: User's entire contact list receives spam invitations without informed consent

text: Your content may be used to improve Figma AI features
rationale: Sneaking/forced action from Figma (early 2025) documented on deceptive.design. All users were automatically opted in to having design files used for AI training. Opt-out required finding and toggling a buried setting. Similar to Meta AI training opt-out controversy.
risk_outcome: Proprietary design files are used for AI training without meaningful user consent

text: 450 Robux for $4.99
rationale: Virtual currency obfuscation targeting children documented on deceptive.design. Converting real money to virtual currency (Robux) disconnects spending from financial reality. Children described the conversion as 'scary' and confusing, leading to unintentional overspending.
risk_outcome: Children overspend real money through confusing virtual currency conversion

text: Subscribe to Premium for push notifications when baby wakes — $9.99/month
rationale: Feature paywall after purchase documented on deceptive.design Hall of Shame. Previously free push notifications locked behind $9.99/month subscription after a hardware purchase ($400). Exploits sunk cost and parental concern to coerce ongoing payments.
risk_outcome: Parent pays recurring subscription to access feature that was free at time of hardware purchase

text: You have a pre-approved personal loan! Get started
rationale: Pre-approved loan trick documented on deceptive.design Hall of Shame. 'Get started' button has a pre-checked consent checkbox above it for credit score checking. User clicks the inviting CTA without noticing they are consenting to a hard credit inquiry.
risk_outcome: User triggers hard credit inquiry thinking they are just viewing loan details

text: 15 people are looking at this property right now
rationale: Booking.com activity message documented in OECD report and deceptive.design. Creates artificial competitive pressure. Numbers are often inflated or fabricated to simulate demand.
risk_outcome: User books immediately fearing property will sell out

text: In high demand! Booked 32 times in the last 24 hours
rationale: High-demand message from Booking.com documented in Princeton study and OECD report. Combines social proof with scarcity to create compound urgency. User cannot verify the booking count.
risk_outcome: User rushes booking without comparing alternatives

text: Your cart will expire in 10:00 minutes, please check out now
rationale: Cart expiry countdown documented in Princeton study on shopping website cart pages. Creates artificial deadline on items that remain available. Timer often resets on page reload.
risk_outcome: User completes checkout without reviewing order to beat fake timer

text: Deal ends in 2:34:56
rationale: AliExpress SuperDeals countdown documented on deceptive.design. Timer appears to expire but identical deals reappear immediately. Same products cycle through SuperDeals indefinitely.
risk_outcome: User impulse buys believing deal is expiring when it cycles perpetually

text: Selling fast! Only 3 left
rationale: Fashion Nova low-stock message documented in Princeton study. Combines demand claim with specific inventory number. Study found some sites randomly generated stock counts on each page load.
risk_outcome: User buys immediately without price comparison due to fabricated scarcity

text: 28 people have added this to their cart
rationale: FTC specifically cited this text as deceptive scarcity. FTC report noted actual number may be 2 when sites display 28. Fabricated cart counts constitute unfair or deceptive acts.
risk_outcome: User perceives false competitive demand and purchases impulsively

text: Prices may increase — this deal is selling out fast!
rationale: Flight booking urgency message combining price threat with scarcity claim. Documented in OECD report as compound urgency tactic. Prices may fluctuate but not due to the specific scarcity claimed.
risk_outcome: User books immediately at current price fearing increase that may not occur

text: Collin P. from Grandview, Missouri just bought this item
rationale: Fake purchase notification from Princeton dark-patterns-at-scale study. Pop-up uses specific name and location to appear authentic. Study found these were generated randomly by third-party scripts.
risk_outcome: User believes product is popular and purchases to avoid missing out

text: 65 people in your area have recently purchased this item
rationale: Geo-targeted fake activity message documented in Princeton study. Combines social proof with local proximity to increase credibility. Numbers are fabricated by third-party popup services.
risk_outcome: User trusts locally-targeted social proof and buys without research

text: 39 other people are viewing this item right now
rationale: FTC cited this specific activity message format as deceptive social proof. Viewer counts are often randomly generated. Creates artificial competition for items with ample supply.
risk_outcome: User feels competitive pressure from fabricated viewer count

text: Hurry! This deal ends at midnight!
rationale: Midnight deadline pattern found across hundreds of ecommerce sites in Princeton study. Same deal typically reappears the next day. Creates false daily urgency cycle.
risk_outcome: User buys before midnight when same deal will return tomorrow

text: Items in your cart are in high demand and selling fast
rationale: Cart-page urgency message cited by FTC. Appears after user has already selected items, exploiting sunk cost. Demand claim is generic and not tied to actual inventory data.
risk_outcome: User rushes checkout to avoid losing items already in cart

text: This product is trending — bought 150 times this week
rationale: Trending badge with specific purchase count from Shopify stores. Princeton study found third-party apps generate these counts. Exact number creates false precision and credibility.
risk_outcome: User purchases based on fabricated popularity metrics

text: Special offer expires in 05:00
rationale: Five-minute countdown popup documented across ecommerce sites. Princeton study found 40% of countdown timers were fake — resetting or looping when they expire.
risk_outcome: User makes snap purchase within 5-minute window that resets anyway

text: Only available for the next 24 hours!
rationale: 24-hour urgency in promotional email. Documented in FTC dark patterns report. Offer typically persists well beyond stated window. Creates artificial daily deadline.
risk_outcome: User clicks through email and purchases under false 24-hour deadline

text: Almost gone! Last chance to buy at this price
rationale: Combined urgency and scarcity message. Vague 'last chance' without specific deadline. OECD report categorizes this as compound dark pattern exploiting both temporal and quantity heuristics.
risk_outcome: User panic-buys product that remains available at same price

text: ★★★★★ Life changing product! — Sarah M., Verified Purchase
rationale: Fake testimonial documented in Princeton study. Researchers found identical reviews with different customer names across multiple sites. 'Verified Purchase' badge lends false credibility.
risk_outcome: User trusts fabricated review and makes purchase based on false social proof

text: Over 10,000 sold! Don't miss out
rationale: Sales count badge creating social proof urgency. Number is unverifiable and often inflated. Pairs social proof with FOMO trigger ('Don't miss out').
risk_outcome: User joins perceived bandwagon based on unverifiable sales figure

text: Your exclusive offer expires today!
rationale: Email subject line creating personalized urgency. 'Exclusive' implies scarcity. 'Today' creates deadline. Same email is often sent repeatedly with rolling expiry dates.
risk_outcome: User opens email and purchases under false personalized deadline

text: Limited stock — selling out fast!
rationale: Generic low-stock message without specific quantity. Princeton study found sites showing this for all products regardless of inventory. Vague enough to always appear plausible.
risk_outcome: User buys without research believing supply is genuinely limited

text: Due to high demand, we can only hold this item for 15 minutes
rationale: Hold timer on booking/ticketing sites documented in StubHub DC AG lawsuit (2024). Frames timer as protecting the user but actually pressures rushed checkout. Items are not actually held exclusively.
risk_outcome: User rushes checkout under fake hold timer without reviewing terms

text: Someone in Los Angeles just purchased this
rationale: Geo-targeted fake purchase popup using visitor's approximate location. Princeton study documented third-party scripts that generate city names from visitor IP. Creates hyper-local false social proof.
risk_outcome: User trusts locally-targeted notification and buys impulsively

text: Last room available at this price!
rationale: Hotel booking scarcity message. Amazon received $8M fine in Poland (2024) for similar tactics. 'Last room at this price' may be technically true but misleading — other rooms at similar prices exist.
risk_outcome: User books hotel room immediately without comparing other options

text: This flash sale ends when the timer hits zero!
rationale: Flash sale with explicit timer claim. Shopify Hurrify app documented to reset timer to start when it hits zero ('evergreen mode'). Explicit promise that sale ends is a verifiable falsehood.
risk_outcome: User buys before timer expires; sale continues indefinitely after

text: 87% claimed — act now before this offer disappears
rationale: Claimed-percentage scarcity for deals and coupons. Specific percentage creates false precision. OECD report notes these counters are often algorithmically generated.
risk_outcome: User redeems offer immediately believing only 13% remains

text: Price goes up in 3... 2... 1...
rationale: SaaS landing page countdown threatening imminent price increase. Creates extreme temporal pressure with dramatic countdown. Price rarely actually increases.
risk_outcome: User subscribes immediately under threat of imminent price increase

text: Only 5 spots left at this rate!
rationale: Digital course fake scarcity. Unlimited digital goods cannot genuinely run out. FTC report highlights fake scarcity for unlimited supply items as particularly deceptive.
risk_outcome: User enrolls in course under false seat limit for digital product

text: Viewed 47 times in the last hour
rationale: View counter on product page. Princeton study found these counters decreased on predictable schedules or were randomly generated. Creates illusion of competitive demand.
risk_outcome: User buys quickly fearing competition from 47 other viewers

text: 12 people are looking at this room right now
rationale: Real-time viewer count on hotel booking site. Documented in OECD report. Creates artificial race condition. User has no way to verify if 12 people are genuinely viewing.
risk_outcome: User books room hastily to beat perceived competition

text: These prices won't be available tomorrow
rationale: Tomorrow-deadline price threat on travel sites. Prices may fluctuate but not necessarily upward. Exploits user inability to verify future pricing.
risk_outcome: User books travel at current price fearing increase that may not materialize

text: 89% of similar items sold out last week — don't wait!
rationale: Historical sell-out statistic to justify current urgency. Unverifiable claim about past inventory creates present-tense fear. User extrapolates past scarcity to current availability.
risk_outcome: User purchases immediately based on unverifiable historical claim

text: Popular choice! This item was booked 8 times today
rationale: Daily booking count on travel platform. Creates social proof urgency with specific daily number. OECD report documents fabricated activity messages as common dark pattern.
risk_outcome: User books immediately believing high daily demand threatens availability

text: This item has been saved by 200+ shoppers. Get it before it's gone!
rationale: Wishlist-based social proof combined with scarcity imperative. Saving an item does not reduce stock, but message implies competitive demand. Conflates interest with purchasing intent.
risk_outcome: User converts from browsing to buying based on others' wishlist activity

text: Price match guarantee expires at midnight
rationale: Price match guarantee with fake midnight expiry. Guarantee typically renews daily. Creates false deadline on a standing policy to prevent comparison shopping.
risk_outcome: User buys immediately to preserve guarantee that never actually expires

text: Last seen price: $89. Current price: $129. Prices change frequently.
rationale: Price history anchor creating urgency through upward trend display. User sees prices rising and fears further increases. Historical prices may be cherry-picked or fabricated.
risk_outcome: User books at current price fearing continued upward trend

text: LIVE: 1,247 people shopping this sale right now
rationale: Sitewide live shopper count creating mass-demand illusion. Large specific number suggests exclusivity at risk. Third-party widgets generate these counts automatically.
risk_outcome: User feels competitive pressure from inflated live shopper count

text: Order within 2 hrs 13 min to get it by tomorrow
rationale: Amazon delivery countdown timer. While delivery windows can be real, the countdown creates urgency that benefits the platform regardless of whether the user truly needs next-day delivery. Borderline — useful info wrapped in urgency framing.
risk_outcome: User makes hasty purchase to hit delivery deadline when standard shipping suffices

text: 🔥 Trending now — 500+ orders in the last 24 hours
rationale: Trending badge with fire emoji and order count. Combines visual urgency (emoji) with specific number to simulate viral demand. Order counts are unverifiable and often fabricated.
risk_outcome: User joins perceived trend based on fabricated order volume

text: No thanks, I hate saving money
rationale: Confirmshaming documented in Princeton study and FTC report. Opt-out forces user to claim they hate saving money. Classic identity-threat manipulation.
risk_outcome: User subscribes to marketing to avoid self-shaming statement

text: No thanks, I already know everything
rationale: Blog newsletter confirmshaming. Opt-out implies arrogance and closed-mindedness. Exploits intellectual humility to guilt users into subscribing.
risk_outcome: User subscribes to newsletter to avoid seeming arrogant

text: No, I'd rather bleed to death
rationale: Extreme confirmshaming variant from MyMedic documented on deceptive.design and Vice. Alternative death-framing opt-out for a medical supply company. Particularly egregious given health context.
risk_outcome: User consents to notifications under extreme emotional duress

text: No thanks, I'm OK with missing out on awesome deals
rationale: Confirmshaming from Majesty Coffee Labor Day sale documented by BuiltIn. Company's NPS dropped 20% after implementing this pattern. Forces user to claim they are OK missing deals.
risk_outcome: User signs up for marketing during sale to avoid FOMO self-identification

text: Are you sure you want to stop personalisation?
rationale: Privacy confirmshaming from Belgian newspaper De Tijd documented on deceptive.design. Green 'Keep personalisation' button exploits color psychology. Question framing makes opting out feel like giving something up.
risk_outcome: User keeps tracking enabled due to confusing button design and guilt framing

text: Maybe later (I like missing out)
rationale: FOMO-based confirmshaming documented in EmailTooltester report. Parenthetical confession format forces user to internally acknowledge they enjoy missing out. Combines delay with self-deprecation.
risk_outcome: User opts in to avoid identifying as someone who likes missing out

text: Your account has been flagged for suspicious activity. Click here to secure it now
rationale: Fear-based social engineering documented by FTC and Keepnet Labs. Vague 'suspicious activity' without specifics triggers panic response. Bypasses rational evaluation by exploiting account loss fear.
risk_outcome: User clicks malicious link and discloses credentials under panic

text: Your account will be locked in 24 hours unless you verify your identity
rationale: Account lockout threat with temporal deadline documented by Proofpoint and Keepnet Labs. Combines fear of account loss with artificial 24-hour deadline to prevent verification of legitimacy.
risk_outcome: User provides credentials on fraudulent site under time pressure

text: Unusual sign-in activity detected on your account
rationale: Fake security alert mimicking Microsoft documented by Abnormal AI. Vague 'unusual activity' creates ambiguous threat. User cannot evaluate severity without clicking through to potentially malicious verification page.
risk_outcome: User clicks verification link on spoofed security page

text: Action required: Your payment method has failed. Update now or lose access
rationale: Payment failure alert pattern documented by Keepnet Labs. Combines financial anxiety with access threat. Legitimate services send these but the pattern is widely exploited in phishing.
risk_outcome: User enters payment details on fraudulent update page

text: We're sorry to see you go. Are you sure you want to lose all your benefits?
rationale: Loss-framed cancellation guilt found in 87.5% of major brands per EmailTooltester study. Combines sadness appeal with benefit-loss threat. Research shows 28% trust reduction from these patterns.
risk_outcome: User abandons cancellation due to combined guilt and loss framing

text: Is this really game over?
rationale: EA cancellation confirmshaming documented in EmailTooltester report. Gaming metaphor frames cancellation as defeat. Creates emotional friction beyond what a neutral confirmation requires.
risk_outcome: User keeps subscription to avoid feeling like they are 'losing'

text: We're always sad to see our members leave
rationale: Qobuz cancellation sadness appeal documented in EmailTooltester report. Anthropomorphizes the service to create interpersonal guilt. User feels they are causing emotional harm to a company.
risk_outcome: User delays cancellation due to manufactured emotional bond with service

text: You'll lose access to all your playlists and saved songs
rationale: Spotify cancellation loss framing. Emphasizes accumulated content at risk rather than monetary savings from canceling. Exploits sunk cost bias around curated music library.
risk_outcome: User keeps subscription to protect playlists they invested time curating

text: Your device may be at risk. Update your security settings immediately
rationale: Fake device security alert documented by Proofpoint. Browser pop-ups mimicking OS warnings to pressure software downloads. Exploits user trust in device-level alerts.
risk_outcome: User downloads unwanted security software or grants unnecessary permissions

text: If you leave now, your selections will not be saved
rationale: Checkout abandonment threat leveraging sunk cost of selections. Creates fear of repeating effort already invested. Documented in OECD dark commercial patterns report.
risk_outcome: User completes checkout to avoid losing configuration effort

text: Your premium features expire tomorrow. Renew now to avoid interruption
rationale: Renewal urgency nagging. Frames non-renewal as losing features rather than ending a paid service. Creates anxiety about workflow disruption to prevent evaluation of alternatives.
risk_outcome: User renews subscription hastily without evaluating alternatives

text: Without an upgrade, you'll be limited to basic features only
rationale: Upgrade loss framing. Frames current free tier as deprivation rather than presenting premium as enhancement. Psychological reframing makes basic features feel inadequate.
risk_outcome: User upgrades to avoid feeling limited rather than for genuine need

text: Your competitors are already using this. Don't fall behind
rationale: B2B fear-based competitive pressure. Unverifiable claim about competitor adoption. Exploits professional anxiety about falling behind to pressure enterprise software purchases.
risk_outcome: Business purchases software based on unverifiable competitor claim

text: Last chance to keep your special pricing before it resets to standard rates
rationale: Price increase threat during cancellation. Documented in EmailTooltester study found in 47.5% of services. Threatens loss of grandfathered pricing to exploit loss aversion.
risk_outcome: User keeps subscription to preserve current pricing regardless of need

text: Your account security score is LOW. Take action to improve it
rationale: Gamified security score designed to create persistent anxiety. 'LOW' label implies danger requiring action. Actions to improve score often involve sharing more data or enabling more features.
risk_outcome: User shares additional personal data to improve arbitrary security score

text: We noticed you haven't logged in recently. Your account may be deactivated
rationale: Inactivity threat email designed to drive re-engagement. Implies account deletion for low activity. Creates anxiety about losing account and data even when deactivation is unlikely.
risk_outcome: User logs in and re-engages with service they intended to abandon

text: Leaving? Your team members will no longer be able to collaborate on shared files
rationale: Team-impact guilt in SaaS cancellation flow. Shifts cancellation consequence from individual to team. Exploits social responsibility to prevent subscription cancellation.
risk_outcome: User keeps subscription out of guilt about impacting team members

text: TikTok would like to send you notifications
rationale: Persistent permission re-request from TikTok documented on hallofshame.design. Despite repeated denial, TikTok keeps asking for notification permission. Wears down user resistance through repetition.
risk_outcome: User grants notification permission to stop repeated interruptions

text: Your PayPal account has been limited. Please confirm your information to restore full access
rationale: PayPal phishing pattern documented by Keepnet Labs. 'Limited' account status creates financial anxiety. Links to spoofed PayPal page harvesting credentials and payment details.
risk_outcome: User enters credentials on fraudulent site to restore account access

text: Your Netflix membership is about to be cancelled. We're having trouble with your current billing information
rationale: Netflix billing phishing pattern documented by Keepnet Labs and Proofpoint. Impersonates Netflix to create service-loss anxiety. Users click through to spoofed billing page. Exploits attachment to streaming library.
risk_outcome: User provides payment details on spoofed Netflix billing page

text: Added to your order: Travel Insurance — $29.99
rationale: Airline sneak-into-basket documented by NNGroup and OECD. Travel insurance auto-added during booking. User must actively locate and remove the item, which is often hidden below the fold.
risk_outcome: User pays for unwanted travel insurance auto-added to booking

text: By continuing, you agree to receive marketing communications
rationale: Buried marketing consent in checkout flow. Continuing purchase auto-opts user into marketing. No separate checkbox — consent is bundled with purchase action. OECD documents this as forced action.
risk_outcome: User unknowingly consents to marketing by completing purchase

text: Your free trial has ended. You've been charged $14.99
rationale: Post-trial auto-charge without adequate warning. FTC 2024 study found forced action (requiring payment info for free trials) in 66.4% of subscription sites. Spotify specifically cited for not notifying before first charge.
risk_outcome: User is charged for subscription they forgot to cancel before trial ended

text: Annual plan — save 50%! (12-month commitment required)
rationale: Adobe-style annual lock-in documented in DOJ/FTC complaint (June 2024). Savings percentage dominates while 12-month commitment and early termination fee are minimized. Monthly price makes it appear flexible.
risk_outcome: User locks into annual commitment believing they have monthly flexibility

text: To cancel, you must first speak with our loyalty team during business hours
rationale: Phone-only cancellation with limited hours documented in FTC Vonage case. Asymmetric friction — online signup but phone-only cancel with retention scripts. Loyalty team is incentivized to prevent cancellation.
risk_outcome: User continues paying because calling during business hours is too inconvenient

text: Send me updates from companies I apply to
rationale: LinkedIn Easy Apply pre-checked checkbox documented on NNGroup and deceptive.design. Auto-subscribes users to company updates during job application. Pre-selection exploits attention scarcity during application process.
risk_outcome: User auto-subscribed to company updates they never intended to follow

text: Subscribe & Save: delivery every 2 weeks
rationale: Amazon Subscribe & Save pre-selected by default on product pages. Discount incentivizes recurring delivery user may not need. Easy to overlook during one-click checkout. Creates ongoing financial commitment.
risk_outcome: User receives recurring deliveries of product intended as one-time purchase

text: Convenience fee: $4.99
rationale: Convenience fee revealed at checkout on ticketing platforms. StubHub DC AG lawsuit (2024) specifically targeted hidden fees. Fee is mandatory despite being labeled as optional 'convenience'.
risk_outcome: User pays mandatory fee disguised as optional convenience

text: Insurance included for your protection
rationale: Pre-selected insurance on rental car booking. Frames unwanted add-on as protective measure using authority language. User must actively deselect. Documented in OECD report as sneak-into-basket variant.
risk_outcome: User pays for redundant insurance already covered by credit card or personal policy

text: Your card will be charged upon trial expiration unless you cancel 48 hours in advance
rationale: 48-hour advance cancellation requirement buried in terms. Creates hidden deadline before visible trial end date. Users who cancel on the last day are still charged. Documented in FTC subscription practices report.
risk_outcome: User is charged because they cancelled within 48 hours of trial end instead of before

text: Seat selection fee: $32.00 per segment
rationale: Airline seat selection drip pricing. Base fare excludes seat selection which is revealed mid-booking. 'Per segment' multiplier further obscures total cost on multi-leg trips.
risk_outcome: User pays $64+ for seat selection on round trip not included in advertised fare

text: Priority boarding added: $19.99
rationale: Pre-selected priority boarding add-on during airline checkout. User must explicitly decline. Positioned alongside required steps so it appears mandatory. Classic sneak-into-basket pattern.
risk_outcome: User pays for priority boarding they never intended to purchase

text: By signing up, you consent to sharing your data with our trusted partners
rationale: Bundled data sharing consent buried in signup flow. 'Trusted partners' is deliberately vague. Consent is tied to account creation so user cannot sign up without agreeing to data sharing.
risk_outcome: User's data shared with unknown third parties as condition of account creation

text: Your Audible credits will be forfeited if you cancel
rationale: Credit forfeiture threat in Audible cancellation flow. Users accumulate unused credits through subscription. Forfeiture creates sunk cost barrier to cancellation. Documented in Princeton cancellation study.
risk_outcome: User keeps subscription to avoid losing credits they already paid for

text: Delivery fee: $5.99 | Service fee: $3.99 | Small order fee: $2.00
rationale: Stacked fees on food delivery platforms. Multiple small fees individually seem minor but collectively add 30-50% to order cost. OECD report documents this as drip pricing compound pattern.
risk_outcome: User pays significantly more than menu price due to stacked hidden fees

text: Upgrade included: Extended warranty — $49.99/year (auto-renews)
rationale: Pre-selected auto-renewing extended warranty during electronics checkout. 'Upgrade included' frames add-on as a bonus rather than additional charge. Auto-renewal creates ongoing commitment from one-time purchase.
risk_outcome: User pays for auto-renewing warranty they never intentionally selected

text: Your contacts will be synced to improve your experience
rationale: Default contact sync framed as UX improvement. LinkedIn $13M settlement for similar contact-harvesting practice. 'Improve your experience' obscures that contacts will be used for growth marketing.
risk_outcome: User's entire contact list is harvested for marketing without informed consent
